chunks: Ali ibn Muhammad ibn Bundar and others, from Ahmad ibn Abi Abdillah al-Barqi, from Ibn Faddal and Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from Ibn al-Qaddah, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

A man came to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) and he said to him: 'Do you have a wife?' He said: 'No.' So he said: 'My father said: I would not prefer that the world and all it contains were mine, if it meant spending a single night without a wife.'

Then he said: 'Two rak'as prayed by a married man are superior to those of an unmarried man who stands in prayer throughout his night and fasts throughout his day.' Then his father gave him seven dinars and said to him: 'Get married with these.'
Then his father said: The Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'Take wives, for it will bring more sustenance to you.'

key_terms.أرزق: More sustaining in provision — marriage brings greater divine sustenance (rizq)
key_terms.أعزب: Celibate/unmarried man — one who has not yet fulfilled the sunnah of marriage
key_terms.اتخذوا الأهل: Take wives/family — a prophetic command to marry, indicating its strong recommendation
key_terms.الركعتان: Two rak'as — the unit of salat prayer, here symbolizing regular worship
key_terms.متزوج: Married man — one who has fulfilled the sunnah of marriage

ai.seo_question: What did Imam al-Sadiq say about the virtue of marriage in Islam?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) narrates a teaching of his father Imam al-Baqir (peace be upon him) strongly emphasizing the virtue and importance of marriage. The hadith presents multiple arguments: marriage is valued over the entire world's wealth, the prayer of a married man surpasses the night-vigil and fasting of an unmarried man, and the Prophet himself commanded believers to marry, promising greater divine provision. This reflects the Shia jurisprudential principle that fulfilling social and familial obligations enhances the spiritual value of worship.
